title: Fit locating pins to a fixture and load a bracket onto them so it is located
instruction: Fit locating pins to the fixture plate and load the bracket onto them so it is located.
context: Machinists (288,300 US jobs) and tool and die makers (56,700 US jobs in 2025; BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook) set up workholding fixtures at every changeover. A part is located by two of its holes: one round pin fixes its position and a relieved "diamond" pin only stops it turning, because the hole spacing of a real part is never exactly the fixture's. Which pins go in which hole, and which way the diamond faces, decide whether the part drops onto its rests or binds on the pin heads, and every cut made afterwards is measured from that location. Real slip fits are about 0.02 mm; a pin set wrongly is only noticed when the part will not seat.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; arm bases at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Everything is square to the table's edges. (1) Fixture plate: bare aluminium, 120 mm along x, 200 mm along y, 20 mm thick, fixed, centred at x 30.0 cm, y 0. Two locating holes 12.4 mm across and 19 mm deep, centres 100.0 mm apart on a line along y: hole A at y +5.0 cm (robot's left), hole B at y -5.0 cm. Each has a 2 mm 45 degree lead-in. Four rest pads 10 x 10 mm and 5 mm tall stand on the plate at x 30.0 +-2.1 cm, y +-5.0 cm. (2) Three loose steel locating pins, 7.85 g/cm3: each has a 12 mm shank 18 mm long, a 22 mm flange 3 mm thick and a 16 mm head 12 mm tall with a lead-in chamfer, 15 mm above the flange's underside to the head top. Two are round (44 g each). The third, the diamond pin (34 g), has a blackened head relieved to two 2 mm lands 16 mm apart on the circle and 8 mm across its flats between them. They hang by their flanges in racks 22 mm tall with 14 mm holes: round pins in the right rack at x 22.0 cm, y -23.5 cm and y -29.5 cm; the diamond in the left rack at x 23.5 cm, y +25.0 cm, its lands along y. A pin pushed home (flange within 0.5 mm of the plate, upright) is locked in its hole there; before that it turns freely. (3) Bracket: blue aluminium, 150 mm (y) x 60 mm (x) x 8 mm thick, 185 g, with two round 16.4 mm holes, a 101.0 mm centre distance (1.0 mm more than the fixture's: a normal error for a welded, fabricated bracket). It lies on two 12 mm rails centred at x 13.5 cm, y +11.0 cm, long side along y. (4) Two black racks and the rails; nothing else is on the table. Checked by calculation: over two round pins the bracket overlaps their heads by 0.3 mm at best and cannot go down; over a round pin and the diamond with its lands square to the line between the holes it goes down with its hole over the round pin within +-0.16 mm and +-0.18 deg, and the diamond may be off square by up to about 45 deg; a diamond turned a quarter turn overlaps by 0.28 mm: a real one binds, but in the simulator the contact give lets the bracket down, so the scorer judges it by the diamond's angle.
scoring: End state, read at the last step from the poses of the three pins and the bracket and from both grippers. A pin is home when its flange is within 0.5 mm of the plate (axis within 3 degrees of vertical, head up) and its axis is within 1 mm of a hole's centre. A located set is one round pin home in one hole and the diamond pin home in the other, its two lands within 15 degrees of square to the line between the holes (measured from above). The bracket is seated when its underside is within 0.3 mm of the rest pads' top (25.0 mm above the table), it is level and square to the line between the holes within 0.3 degrees, and its hole over the round pin has its centre within 0.3 mm of that pin's axis (its located pose: with the round pin in B the bracket's centre is 0.5 mm to the left of the fixture's centre, with it in A 0.5 mm to the right). Both grippers are clear when every finger zone is at least 25 mm from the bracket and every pin. Still: over the last 1 s the bracket's centre and its hole centres move under 0.3 mm and it turns under 0.3 degrees. Score 0 if a pin or the bracket is off the table (centre outside the table's outline, or lowest point more than 10 mm below the table top). Otherwise: 1.0 for a located set home with the bracket seated, both grippers clear and still; 0.5 for a located set home with the bracket not seated (held, resting on the pin heads, on the table, or off its pose); 0.25 for any one pin home without a located set (two round pins, the diamond turned wrong, one pin only; a bracket seated over such pins earns only this); 0 otherwise. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Success: 1.0 held for 1 s. In a real trial: a feeler gauge and dial indicator on the bracket, a photo from above for the diamond.
fidelity: Real slip fits are about 0.02 mm; the model uses 0.4 mm (12.4 in 12.0, 16.4 in 16.0) because the physics engine cannot resolve finer. Round holes are 16-sided rings of turned boxes. The diamond's lands are boxes. The lock is a rule that rewrites a home pin's pose each step, standing for a ball detent or press fit. Rigid bodies, friction 0.4. The 1.0 mm spacing error is ours: large enough that two round pins overlap by more than the simulator's contact give.
reset_notes: Hang the round pins in the right rack (x 22.0 cm, y -23.5 and -29.5 cm), the diamond pin in the left rack (x 23.5 cm, y +25.0 cm) with its lands along y; lay the bracket on its rails centred at x 13.5 cm, y +11.0 cm, long side along y. Both fixture holes empty, no pin locked: release any detent. Nothing is consumed.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; demo: 1.0; left arm alone: 0.25; right arm alone: 0.25
